content.text:
As of **29 September 2026**, these are three different kinds of memory assistant. The key distinction is what they observe: **Hemory hears conversations; Littlebird and Goldfish read text exposed by desktop apps.**

| Product | Capture and memory | How questions are answered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **[Hemory](https://www.hemory.com/features/)** | Records audio on iPhone or Apple Watch when listening is enabled. It transcribes and labels speakers, splits conversations into activities, makes summaries, and derives semantic vectors and relationships. It explicitly describes a **memory graph** built from transcripts. It does not currently claim desktop screen reading. [Features](https://www.hemory.com/features/), [terms](https://www.hemory.com/legal/terms/), [privacy](https://www.hemory.com/legal/privacy/) | Its built-in agent searches past transcript passages to answer across conversations. It also exposes memory search to external agents through MCP. [Features](https://www.hemory.com/features/) |
| **[Littlebird](https://littlebird.ai/)** | Every few seconds, its desktop app reads text and interface elements in the **active window** through accessibility permissions; it also transcribes meetings and can pull more data from authorized integrations. It says it takes no screenshots or video. Captured memory is indexed and stored encrypted in AWS, rather than solely on your computer. [Capture explanation](https://littlebird.ai/blog/what-does-littlebird-actually-see), [storage explanation](https://littlebird.ai/blog/is-littlebird-safe) | Chat searches that history, meeting notes, Projects, and editable Assistant Notes; MCP can expose the memory to other AI clients. Littlebird describes a searchable index, **not a confirmed graph database or graph schema**. [Knowledge-base explanation](https://littlebird.ai/blog/personal-knowledge-base-with-ai), [MCP](https://littlebird.ai/features/mcp) |
| **[Goldfish](https://docs.goldfish.sh/)** | Reads text in the active app through accessibility APIs, without screenshots or screen recording. It stores captured text and generated memory in a **local SQLite database**. It automatically creates browsable, connected wiki pages for people, projects, topics, tools, and organizations. That is a graph-like user view; its underlying graph implementation is not documented. [Privacy policy](https://goldfish.sh/privacy), [Memory settings](https://docs.goldfish.sh/reference/settings/) | Its chat retrieves local memory to answer questions or draft text. A local MCP server lets other desktop AI clients search that memory. Selected context also goes to Goldfish’s Azure OpenAI service for answers **and background memory organization**, despite the database remaining local. [Chat](https://docs.goldfish.sh/guides/chat/), [MCP](https://docs.goldfish.sh/guides/ai-clients/), [privacy](https://goldfish.sh/privacy) |

The likely shared pattern is **capture → filter and organize → index → retrieve relevant records for a question → have a model compose an answer**. That is an architectural inference from their published descriptions, not a claim that they use the same pipeline. In particular, accessibility reading depends on what an app exposes as text; it is not equivalent to understanding every pixel or reading every hidden document in an app.

### Bring your own model

**I found no documented OpenRouter key or general “choose your model” setting for any of the three built-in assistants.** Their MCP interfaces offer a different route: use the memory **from an external AI client**, whose model and billing you choose. That does not replace the model used internally to transcribe, organize, or answer inside the product.

- **Hemory:** External agents can query its read-only MCP memory tool. Its hosted AI processing uses providers selected by Hemory; a local inference provider is described for self-hosting, while the product site still lists self-hosting as coming soon. [MCP and availability](https://www.hemory.com/features/), [AI terms](https://www.hemory.com/legal/terms/)
- **Littlebird:** Its remote MCP service lets compatible clients query its memory. Its [facts page](https://littlebird.ai/facts) says MCP requires **Power or above**, although the [MCP feature page](https://littlebird.ai/features/mcp) inconsistently says “Plus and above” in one section. Check the account’s current entitlement before paying for that use.
- **Goldfish:** Its **local** MCP server works with local MCP clients, including Claude Desktop, Cursor, and Claude Code according to its docs. An OpenRouter-backed client could use it **if that client supports local stdio MCP**. [AI client guide](https://docs.goldfish.sh/guides/ai-clients/)

A **ChatGPT subscription is not an API key or a pool of API usage**; OpenAI bills API calls separately. [OpenAI billing guide](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9039756-managing-billing-settings-on-the-chatgpt-web-and-api-platform) ChatGPT can use some custom **remote** MCP apps depending on plan and permissions, but cannot directly connect to Goldfish’s local MCP server without an additional tunnel or remote adapter. I did not verify a working ChatGPT connection to any of these three. [OpenAI MCP guide](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12584461-developer-mode-and-mcp-apps-in-chatgpt)

**Practical choice:** Hemory fits spoken, real-world conversations; Littlebird fits broad desktop and meeting recall with cloud storage; Goldfish fits desktop text recall with a local memory database. If OpenRouter control is the deciding factor, look at their **MCP access as the supported seam**, while treating their own internal model pipeline as vendor-managed.

content.text:
I’d build **M Graph as a local macOS service with its own data store and API**. Memotron would consume that API, and local agents would use a read-only MCP server. There’s no need for an M Graph chat UI.

```text
macOS Accessibility
    → observations → deduplicated activities → evidence-backed graph
                                               ↘ clusters and groups
                                  → local API → Memotron
                                  → stdio MCP → local agents
```

### What I found in the existing work

The [mgraph prototype](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/mgraph/README.md) already has useful ideas: source hashes, claims tied to quoted passages, judged relationships, stable clusters, broader cluster groups, and read-only MCP tools. I would preserve those **data contracts and clustering rules**. Its current ingestion and storage are tied to DynamoDB, R2, hosted Postgres, and specific inference providers, so I would not put the whole prototype inside a desktop app unchanged. Its reported evaluation is also too small to establish graph quality yet.

Memotron’s macOS host is a native SwiftUI app around a web view. Its current [entitlements](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/ios/memotron/Memotron%20for%20Mac/Memotron_for_Mac.entitlements) enable App Sandbox. That matters: [Apple lists accessibility APIs used by assistive apps as incompatible with App Sandbox](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/protecting-user-data-with-app-sandbox). The first engineering spike should therefore prove capture in a **separate, signed native helper** with Accessibility permission, and prove its connection to Memotron. We should not assume the existing sandboxed host can perform capture itself.

### The core I would build

1. **Native capture adapter.** Observe the active app and accessibility tree, using notifications where available and throttled reads where necessary. Record app, window, time, available document or URL identity, and readable text. Deduplicate repeated views. Give users app exclusions, pause, and deletion controls from the start. Accessibility data depends on what each app exposes; it is not a complete record of everything on screen.

2. **Local evidence store.** Start with SQLite for observations, source identity, full-text search, graph records, and processing state. Treat an observation as evidence, not automatically as a memory node. Group repeated views into activities or documents; derive entities, claims, and relationships with references back to the text and observation time. Keep derived records versioned so a changed model can rebuild them.

3. **Graph processor.** Adapt the prototype’s candidate selection, relation judgments, clusters, and cluster groups to the local store. Run capture and deterministic deduplication while offline; queue model work separately. Test cluster stability and false connections on a reviewed sample of real data before broad indexing.

4. **Two consumers of one core.** Expose a small local API to Memotron through its native bridge, with a separate adapter for existing Memotron entries if desired. Expose read-only MCP tools such as `search`, `read`, `related`, `get_cluster`, and `list_groups`. Results should include source, observation time, supporting passages, and whether a link was judged or merely suggested. The existing [MCP server](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/mgraph/mgraph/mcp_server.py) is a good starting contract; the desktop packaging needs its own verification.

I would keep the capability independent of Nucleus and Subset. Memotron should own its product integration; Subset can list a standalone surface only after its actual installer and flow work. I also checked Superfunctions’ `mcpfn` package as required by the repository guide: it is worth evaluating if the adapter is written in TypeScript, but it does not justify rewriting a working Python MCP contract by itself.

### Models and privacy

**OpenRouter is a practical first provider.** It documents both [embedding requests](https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/typescript/api-reference/embeddings) and [schema-constrained outputs for supported models](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/structured-outputs). I’d make embedding, claim extraction, relationship judgment, and labeling separate configurable model roles. Validate every response locally, record model/version and cost, and set processing budgets. Store the API key in Keychain. Because captured text may be sensitive, sending it to OpenRouter should require an explicit per-app or per-source choice; capture can remain local without inference.

**ChatGPT subscription support needs a narrower experiment.** [Aside advertises subscription support](https://aside.com/), and [OpenAI documents programmatic Codex SDK access through supported ChatGPT plans](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/pricing). That gives us a legitimate route to test a subscription-backed processor. It does not establish a general subscription-funded embeddings API or that continuous background graph enrichment is a good fit for Codex. I would first let a subscribed Codex agent *query* M Graph through MCP, then prototype low-volume graph processing through the Codex SDK and measure throughput, limits, reliability, and structured-result quality. OpenRouter remains the initial indexing provider.

### Suggested sequence

- **Spike:** prove Accessibility capture and helper packaging against a few representative apps, including Memotron’s sandboxed host.
- **First usable release:** local capture, deduplication, searchable evidence, deletion controls, and working MCP connections in two local agent hosts.
- **Graph release:** OpenRouter processing, evidence-backed relations, clusters and groups, with a reviewed quality set.
- **Memotron integration:** consume the same graph and decide whether existing saved Memotron entries join it.
- **Provider expansion:** test the Codex subscription adapter and other model routes against the same processor contract.

Two choices most affect the design: **should the first release keep all captured data and graph storage on the Mac, with only selected inference requests sent to OpenRouter; and is direct signed macOS distribution acceptable for the capture helper?** I’d proceed with both as the working assumptions. I’d also include existing Memotron entries as a later source adapter unless you want them in the first graph release.

This was a read-only architecture review; I made no repository changes.

Memotron owns the feature and its lifecycle. M Graph is reusable **code and a local protocol**, so another app could package it later; it is not a separately installed prerequisite. Local agents would connect to the MCP executable at a path inside `Memotron.app`.

I’ll map the existing mgraph code into a standalone service boundary: what can stay as graph logic, what needs a local store and capture process, and what Memotron would later bundle unchanged.

Build **M Graph as a self-contained local runtime**. Its standalone app starts that runtime; later, Memotron bundles and starts the **same runtime**. Memotron does not become the graph engine, and users do not install M Graph separately to use Memotron.

### Runtime boundary

| Component | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `mgraph-capture` | Swift macOS process that reads permitted Accessibility data and emits observations |
| `mgraphd` | Sole owner of the local database, processing queue, graph, clusters, settings, and deletion |
| `mgraph-mcp` | Small stdio adapter that connects local agents to `mgraphd` with read-only tools |
| Standalone shell | Minimal onboarding and controls: permission, app selection, pause, status, and deletion; no chat |

Use a **versioned local protocol** between capture and `mgraphd`, and between `mgraphd` and its consumers. That is the reuse boundary. The standalone distribution contains all components; Memotron can later contain the same components and provide its own controls.

### Build it in vertical slices

**1. Prove capture and packaging first.** Build the Swift Accessibility collector and a self-contained development bundle. Check several real apps for text quality, document identity, repeated UI chrome, and permission behavior. Also prove the collector can run with the intended signing arrangement: [Apple’s sandbox restriction](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/protecting-user-data-with-app-sandbox) affects the existing Memotron host. This spike prevents us from committing to a runtime that is awkward to bundle.

**2. Store observations locally before using a model.** `mgraphd` writes to SQLite. Keep immutable observations with app, window/document identity, time, text hash, and capture status. Merge repeated views into an activity or document record; scrolling through the same page must not create hundreds of memories. Add full-text search, exclusions, pause, retention, and deletion. The first MCP tools can already search and read this evidence.

**3. Derive the graph asynchronously.** Add separate jobs for passage extraction, cited claims, embeddings, candidate relationships, judged relationships, clusters, and cluster groups. Every derived item records its source hash, model, version, and supporting passage. Failed or offline inference leaves the captured evidence searchable. Rebuild only derivations affected by changed sources or models.

**4. Start with OpenRouter.** Give profiling, embeddings, pair judgment, and labeling distinct configurable model roles. Require validated structured results and put budgets on background jobs. The user chooses which captured apps may send text to a model provider; API credentials live in Keychain.

**5. Expose a small read-only MCP surface.** Start with `search_memories`, `read_memory`, `nearby_memories`, `get_cluster`, `list_groups`, and `status`. Return evidence and observation times so an agent can distinguish a captured fact from a model-suggested connection. Keep capture settings and deletion in the owner’s local control interface, not in the initial agent tools.

### What to reuse from the prototype

I’d keep the existing Python implementation for the **first graph daemon**, extracting the relatively pure passage validation and clustering logic from [profile_quality.py](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/mgraph/mgraph/profile_quality.py) and [cluster_projection.py](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/mgraph/mgraph/cluster_projection.py). I’d replace its hosted Postgres/R2/DynamoDB access with local repository interfaces. The current [cluster pipeline](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/mgraph/mgraph/cluster_pipeline.py) and [query layer](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/mgraph/mgraph/query.py) mix algorithms with hosted storage, so they need separation rather than wholesale copying.

That gives us Swift for the OS-specific part and Python for graph logic already under test. **A self-contained Python runtime inside the standalone bundle is an early acceptance test.** If that proves unreliable or too costly to maintain, we can move the daemon after the data and IPC contracts are established, without rewriting capture or consumer integrations.

The one decision I’d make now: **start capture with an explicit app allowlist**, including the foreground window only. Is that the behavior you want for the first release, or should recording cover all accessible apps once the user enables it?

I retrieved the hosted **`21n/linear-backlog-architect@1.0.0`** skill and checked the existing Linear backlog. Here is the proposed delivery shape. This is a **planning pass**: I have not changed Linear or queued work.

## Backlog boundary

Create a new **Subset parent issue: “Deliver M Graph as a local macOS memory service.”** Its completion gate is a standalone, self-contained installation that automatically records permitted foreground app context, builds a local evidence-backed graph and clusters, and serves it through read-only local MCP. The runtime must have a versioned interface and packaging layout that Memotron can later bundle without requiring another user installation.

Keep [TIDY-481](https://linear.app/21n/issue/TIDY-481/m-graph) linked as related work, not as the parent or a blocker. It currently plans a graph over **saved Memotron items**, with DataFn and hosted Postgres assumptions. This new effort starts with **local Accessibility capture and SQLite**. The two should share evidence and graph concepts where proven, but neither storage design should silently become the other’s requirement. The completed [NPX-31 Accessibility POC](https://linear.app/21n/issue/NPX-31/accessibility-and-context-awareness-poc) is prior research, not proof of a shippable collector.

| Order | Proposed child issue | Depends on | Readiness | Observable acceptance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Prove Accessibility capture and self-contained runtime packaging | — | **Ready** | A signed development bundle captures useful text in representative apps, handles permission denial/revocation, and runs without a separately installed Python or service dependency. Document sandbox and signing findings. |
| B | Define versioned observation, evidence, graph, and local IPC contracts | — | **Ready** | Schemas cover source identity, time, hashes, cited passages, derived versions, partial states, and deletion. Contract tests reject invalid messages and preserve compatibility across a version change. |
| C | Implement local store and restart-safe job lifecycle | B | **Ready** | SQLite migrations, single-writer ownership, checkpoints, stale-job rejection, and delete/rebuild paths pass restart and upgrade tests. No hosted database is needed. |
| D | Capture permitted foreground context with user controls | A, B, C | **Needs decision** | App selection, pause, permission state, sensitive-field handling, and deletion work in a native test app. Repeated AX reads do not flood storage. Decide the initial app selection policy below. |
| E | Turn observations into stable activities and cited evidence | C, D | **Ready** | Repeated scrolling/window visits consolidate correctly; distinct documents remain distinct; every extracted passage resolves to a captured source and time. Missing text stays marked partial. |
| F | Build an evaluation set and graph quality harness | B, E | **Ready** | A reviewed set includes duplicates, close neighbors, hard negatives, cross-app continuation, and unrelated activity. Report candidate recall, citation support, relation errors, cluster stability, cost, and latency before setting launch thresholds. |
| G | Add opt-in OpenRouter profiling and graph derivation | E, F | **Ready** | Configurable model roles produce locally validated profiles, embeddings, judged relations, clusters, and groups. Jobs respect source/model versions, budgets, offline retry, and provider egress selection. Reuse the prototype’s pure logic where its tests still apply. |
| H | Serve local queries through read-only MCP | C, E; graph tools also need G | **Ready** | A stdio client in two actual local agent hosts can search/read evidence and traverse relationships and clusters. Results identify source, observation time, and inferred versus judged links; no query triggers an unbounded model run. |
| I | Integrate and verify the standalone M Graph app | A–H | **Ready for an internal build** | One installation owns startup, permission onboarding, settings, pause, database, and MCP executable. Verify quit/restart, offline use, removal, upgrade, and a representative end-to-end capture-to-agent query. Public download remains a separate release check. |
| J | Bundle the verified runtime in Memotron | I | **Deferred** | Memotron installs once, starts the bundled runtime, exposes automatic recording controls, and preserves the standalone graph/MCP contracts. Validate its actual signed host and permissions separately. |

**Dependency DAG:** `A → D`; `B → C → D → E`; `B + E → F`; `E + F → G`; `C + E → H`, then add graph reads after `G`; `A–H → I → J`. A, B, and early evaluation design can proceed in parallel. Parent/child hierarchy would not substitute for these blocked-by links.

The smallest first implementation slice is **A + B + C + a narrow D**: one permitted app, local observations, and a restart-safe store. That establishes the service boundary before spending heavily on inference or clustering. The current [mgraph pilot](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/mgraph/README.md) supplies tested passage and clustering ideas, but its hosted storage pipeline is not the local runtime.

I found no M Graph project in the shared Linear implementation loop configuration, so **none of these are queue-ready yet**, even where the technical issue contract is ready. Existing dirty work in Subset and mgraph was left untouched.

**Decision needed for D:** I recommend an explicit **app allowlist** for the first release, with foreground windows only. If you want all accessible apps recorded after one global enable action, D’s privacy controls and acceptance checks change materially.
